newsitem.title: USA: Dole caps campaign journey with vote, chicken soup.
newsitem.headline: Dole caps campaign journey with vote, chicken soup.

text.p: After a final marathon campaign run that ended on Tuesday, Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole cast his ballot in the town he calls the wellspring of his political values.
Surrounded by relatives and friends, he entered the flag-draped First Christian Church in his hometown in the central Kansas plains to vote on an old-fashioned paper ballot.

Since his Depression-era upbringing taught him that modesty was a virtue, he seemed a bit awkward. "I've voted before here lots ... but never voted for myself for president. I was a little nervous," Dole said after he and his wife, Elizabeth, left the polling booths.

Dole had done everything by the book, giving his name to election officials and the address of the house in Russell where he grew up, 1035 N. Maple St. One official, LaRue Covalt, carefully recited the spelling of his name. "Dole. D-O-L-E. Robert. R-O-B-E-R-T."

Afterwards, Dole headed over to the Maple Street house, a small one-story brick building, for some chicken soup and angel food cake with friends and family. He passed the cake around to the group, which included his daughter Robin, two sisters and his close adviser John McCain, the Republican senator from Arizona.
Then he went back out on the street and in a voice that sometimes choked with emotion he thanked his supporters, those who were standing there and others across the country.

"It's always good to be back to Russell, good to be home again. I guess I think the arguments about the election are over. The choice now rests with the voters of America, and I've never doubted their wisdom," Dole said.
"We've had a long uplifting journey, across America. We've given our all but with a full heart. We're ready now to go back to Washington and get ready for the victory party, right?"

Dole has repeatedly cited Russell, which got its start as an oil town late in the last century, as the source of bedrock values on which his political career was based. He was born there 73 years ago to a family of limited means that had to move into the basement of their house for a while to pay the mortgage by renting out the top floor.
It was in Russell that Dole recovered from devastating wounds suffered in the Second World War, and it was his friends and neighbours in Russell who collected money to help pay for his recovery.

At his final campaign stop hours earlier in Independence, Missouri, Dole said the values he learned in Russell would carry him to an upset victory polls have said he would be denied. And he said that in casting his vote in Russell, "I will know that this campaign has been rooted in the most important American ideals: duty, honour, country and integrity."
"The tide of this election, I believe, was turned in diners and bowling alleys, in the heart of a people where the old values endure," he said.

Dole wrapped up a 96-hour, non-stop "march to victory" in Independence before a courthouse statue of Harry Truman, the Democrat who pulled off one of America's greatest political upsets when he defied opinion polls to defeat Republican Tom Dewey in 1948.
"What was true for Harry Truman in 1948 will be true for Bob Dole and Jack Kemp in 1996," the former senator from Kansas said.
Election eve surveys gave Clinton leads ranging from about seven percentage points in a Reuters poll to 18 in a CBS/New York Times survey, with most in-between.

In Dole's last campaign swing, which began on Friday, he made 29 stops in 19 states, covering 10,534 miles (16,950 km). He kept up a breakneck pace around the clock, stopping for only a few hours of sleep in his last-ditch bid to defeat Clinton. He was to return to Washington to await the returns.

Before travelling to Russell from Kansas City, Dole told reporters he had reflected on the campaign as it drew to a close. "It's unique, obviously, and exciting in a way, and I'll be proud to cast my vote. I've worked pretty hard and I'm honoured to be the standard bearer for the party. It's a great responsibility and challenge. I think about all those things."
